$comment: Hand-written catalogue entries. Wins every slug collision against steam-tier.json. Each entry records where its executable names came from and how far they should be trusted. HAND-EDITABLE -- unlike steam-tier.json, this file is not regenerated.
$rules: processNames are BARE filenames. The client resolves them against running processes and takes the real path, so a name that is wrong reports as not-found rather than silently half-routing a game.
No name may appear in generic-names.json. The validator fails the seed on one, because a generic name routes whatever unrelated software happens to be running under it.
Where a publisher's own pages disagree on a spelling, list BOTH. Exactly one will ever resolve on a given machine, and guessing wrong leaves part of a game outside the tunnel with nothing said.
Where a game launches through an anti-cheat wrapper, list the wrapper AND the real binary. The wrapper is what the store launches; the game binary is what carries gameplay traffic.
Never set prefixComplete or destinationCidrs here. No entry in this file has a researched prefix list.

"first-party" grades the SOURCE, not the truth. A publisher support article can be templated across titles and name a file that is not on disk -- Amazon's Lost Ark article names LostArkLauncher.exe, which no observed install contains. Where a first-party page and an observed install disagree, ship BOTH and say so here. A name that does not exist reports as not-found and costs nothing; dropping the real one leaves the game outside the tunnel with nothing said.

The BattlEye '<Game>_BE.exe' convention is a hint, never an inference. BattlEye's own FAQ says 'often named', and Destiny 2 breaks it outright with destiny2launcher.exe. Do not generate a _BE name for a title where one was not observed.

games.source: Discord release channel naming; corroborated
games.notes: Not a game, and catalogued anyway: OONI measured discord.com confirmed-blocked in Iran on 67% of 12,571 consumer measurements, which makes it the single most-blocked entry in this catalogue. Discord's Squirrel updater is named Update.exe and is deliberately NOT listed -- every Electron application on the machine ships that name.

games.source: BattlEye FAQ, https://www.battleye.com/support/faq/ (read 2026-08-25)
games.notes: Its own row rather than a name repeated across every BattlEye title, because that is what it is: one Windows service in C:\Program Files (x86)\Common Files\BattlEye, shared by every BattlEye game on the machine. Attaching it to a single game's row would imply it is part of that game and would route it for all the others anyway. Two research passes disagreed about whether the FAQ names these binaries; the page was read directly and it does, in both the Common Files path and the per-game BattlEye directory.

games.notes: Valve's launch config for this app names only Easy Anti-Cheat's start_protected_game.exe, so the generated tier could not carry this title at all. games.source: Valve client manifest (media.steampowered.com/client/steam_client_win32) and Valve's own firewall article; three of the five names OBSERVED running, rig 2026-08-26
games.notes: VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL INSTALL, 2026-08-26 -- the first row in this catalogue that has been. Steam was installed on the Neoxify-Test2 rig from Valve's own signed installer and run to its login window; the service's own listRunningApps reported steam.exe at C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\, steamservice.exe at C:\Program Files (x86)\Common Files\Steam\ (a different install root, which is why a basename match and not a path guess is the right design), and steamwebhelper.exe at C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\bin\cef\cef.win64\. Six steamwebhelper processes were running and all six shared one image name, so the CEF fan-out needs no extra entry. Nothing else Steam-related was running that this row does not name. steamwebhelper.exe was previously flagged as the weakest name here -- Valve names the process in its client update notes but never prints the string with a .exe suffix, and it is in no enumerable client package -- and it was right; it is also where most of the client's traffic goes. steamchina.exe and streaming_client.exe did not resolve, which is correct rather than a defect: one is the Chinese client and the other exists only during Remote Play. Both are kept, because a name that is not running reports as not-found and costs nothing. Valve's casing SteamService.exe is preserved as they write it. Pinned by the rig-observed test in apps/desktop-windows/src/lib/game-apps.test.ts.
